title: Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS & FaaS
summary: The abstraction spectrum from raw VMs to fully managed apps, and exactly who manages what at each layer.

slides.markdown:
Every cloud offering sits somewhere on a ladder of **how much the provider manages for you** versus how much you still own.

Think of it like eating: **IaaS** is buying groceries and cooking yourself, **PaaS** is a meal-kit where ingredients are prepped, **SaaS** is ordering takeout, and **FaaS** is grabbing a single bite exactly when you're hungry and paying only for that bite.

- Same underlying compute, different slices of responsibility.
- The layer you pick trades **control** for **speed**.

slides.subTitle: On-prem to FaaS
slides.markdown:
The models form a strict ladder of increasing abstraction: **on-prem** (you own the building and the racks) → **IaaS** (you rent VMs, storage, networking) → **PaaS** (you rent a runtime — push code, the platform handles the OS and scaling) → **SaaS** (you rent a finished application) → **FaaS** (you rent a single function invocation).

Each rung up removes a layer of operational burden but also removes a layer of control. A team rarely lives on one rung — a typical company runs IaaS VMs, a PaaS database, and a few SaaS tools, all at once.

"As a service" always means **one specific layer of undifferentiated heavy lifting is now someone else's job** — not that all ops work vanishes.

Running your own database means patching the OS, tuning the engine, managing failover, and taking backups. A managed database-as-a-service takes over patching, failover, and backups — but you still design the schema, write the queries, and size the instance. The removed layer is always **operational toil**, never **your domain decisions**.

slides.subTitle: Raw compute you provision and patch
slides.markdown:
**IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service) gives you virtualized compute, storage, and networking as raw building blocks — a VM, a disk, a subnet. You choose the OS, install and patch it, configure the runtime, and manage scaling yourself.

Example: an EC2 instance running Ubuntu, where you SSH in, install your app's dependencies, and set up your own monitoring. Maximum control, maximum ops burden — you own everything above the hypervisor.

slides.subTitle: A managed runtime you just push code to
slides.markdown:
**PaaS** (Platform as a Service) hands you a ready-made runtime — you push code, and the platform provisions the server, installs the language runtime, and often handles scaling and load balancing for you.

Example: deploying a Node.js app to Heroku or a managed app-runtime service — no server to SSH into, no OS to patch. You trade some control (can't tweak kernel settings) for a much shorter path from code to a running, scaled service.

slides.subTitle: Consuming a finished product
slides.markdown:
**SaaS** (Software as a Service) is a complete application delivered over the internet — you don't provision anything at all, you just use it. Gmail, Salesforce, Slack.

The provider owns everything: servers, runtime, application code, and upgrades. Your only levers are configuration and, sometimes, integrations via an API. This is the far end of the ladder — zero infrastructure decisions, but also zero infrastructure control.

slides.subTitle: Serverless functions
slides.markdown:
**FaaS** (Function as a Service) is PaaS taken to its logical extreme: you don't even manage a running server process — you upload a function, and the platform runs it only when triggered, then tears it down.

Example: an AWS Lambda function that resizes an image whenever one lands in a storage bucket. You pay per invocation, not per idle hour, and scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent runs is automatic. The trade-off is less control over execution environment and cold-start latency.

slides.subTitle: Who secures what
slides.markdown:
Every layer splits security duties between provider and customer, and the split moves as you go up the ladder.

![Shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS](assets/shared-responsibility.svg)

The provider always secures the physical layer — data centers, hardware, the hypervisor. You always secure your data and access control. Everything in between (OS, network config, app code) shifts hands as you move from IaaS toward SaaS.

slides.subTitle: Control vs speed
slides.markdown:
| | IaaS | PaaS | SaaS/FaaS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to first deploy | Slow — provision, patch, configure | Fast — push code | Instant — just use it, or upload a function |
| Control | Full (OS, kernel, network) | Partial (app + config) | Minimal to none |
| Best for | Custom stacks, legacy migration, special compliance | Standard web apps, fast iteration | Commodity needs, event-driven bursts |

**How to decide:** ask what you're actually trying to differentiate on. A startup building a novel product usually wants PaaS/FaaS speed; a bank running a proprietary trading system needs IaaS control.

slides.subTitle: "Serverless means no ops"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Serverless means there's no operations work left for my team."

**Why it's wrong:** FaaS removes server management, not operations. You still own observability (tracing across dozens of short-lived function invocations is harder, not easier), cold-start latency tuning, cost control (a runaway recursive trigger can rack up a huge bill fast), and IAM permissions per function.

**Correct model:** every "as a service" layer shifts *which* ops tasks you do, not whether you do ops at all.

slides.subTitle: Structuring an IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS answer
slides.markdown:
When asked to differentiate the models, don't just recite definitions — anchor each one to **what you'd have to do yourself** and give one concrete product per layer: "IaaS is an EC2 VM I patch myself; PaaS is something like a managed app-runtime where I just push code; SaaS is Gmail — I do nothing but use it."

Then close with the trade-off in one line: control decreases and velocity increases as you climb the ladder. That structure — definition, example, trade-off — reads as fluency, not memorization.
